title: Jarrad Branthwaite is injured again. Where does that leave him and Everton? - The Athletic
description:
The sight of an injured Jarrad Branthwaite limping through the media room on crutches, with his right leg in a brace, did little to improve the tone.
Everton manager David Moyes briefly consoled Branthwaite with an empathetic pat and some words of encouragement as he was taken down the tunnel.
Fans attempted to rally behind a key player, chanting “There’s only one Jarrad Branthwaite” as he was carried off the pitch.
Branthwaite adds balance, allowing Everton to push higher up the pitch and be more aggressive in their play.
Branthwaite and Everton will now spend the next couple of months trying to find ways to end this cycle of misery.
text:
The mood inside Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium after their Merseyside derby loss on Sunday was sombre.

Ashen-faced officials walked around in near silence as they attempted to come to terms with a crushing late defeat, sealed by Virgil van Dijk’s 100th-minute header, that damaged Everton’s hopes of European qualification.

The sight of an injured Jarrad Branthwaite limping through the media room on crutches, with his right leg in a brace, did little to improve the tone. Such measures are standard procedure for most injured players after matches, but the early prognosis on the 23-year-old defender had not been positive.

It was Branthwaite’s reaction to his 87th-minute injury that had caused most concern. He had been limping earlier in the second half, briefly dropping to the turf before attempting to continue, but later slid into the pitchside advertising hoardings after a challenge with Cody Gakpo and stayed down holding his hamstring.

After a lengthy pause for treatment, he was in tears and pulled his shirt over his face as he was taken off by stretcher. Everton manager David Moyes briefly consoled Branthwaite with an empathetic pat and some words of encouragement as he was taken down the tunnel.

Fans attempted to rally behind a key player, chanting “There’s only one Jarrad Branthwaite” as he was carried off the pitch. They and Moyes already know that far too well.

Branthwaite’s injury was not only a sobering setback for a player who has struggled with persistent fitness issues — mainly muscular — but also a significant blow to Everton’s dreams of playing in continental competition next season.

“We are worried,” Moyes said in his post-match press conference, before pointing out that further assessments would be needed to determine the precise extent and severity of Branthwaite’s latest problem.

Even at that early stage, the assumption was that his season, with only five games left, was almost certainly over. Most of the debate centred on whether this issue was as serious as the previous ones — also with his right hamstring — that led to him missing the first half of the campaign, and what that will mean for his pre-season schedule, given the importance of players taking part in a full programme.

Everton’s players and staff were off on Monday, as is usual on the day after a game, but Branthwaite went for a scan to assess the damage.

The results confirmed those fears that he probably won’t play in any of those remaining five fixtures, but there is more optimism now about his prospects of returning for pre-season, provided he encounters no setbacks during his rehabilitation. The general sense from those close to the situation is that the injury is not as bad as first feared.

Everton announced on Wednesday that no surgery would be needed this time, adding “the injury is unrelated to the hamstring area which required surgery in October”. They said Branthwaite was unlikely to feature again this season.

The injury ends Branthwaite’s hopes of making England’s World Cup squad for this summer’s tournament in North America. That was always a long shot, but he had been pushing for selection.

The possibility of him returning for Everton’s summer schedule has at least brought some relief after Sunday’s painful scenes, but the attention now turns to Branthwaite’s treatment, as well as the repercussions — short and long term — for both player and club.

For now, Everton have to find a way through the rest of their season without someone who is an important figure from a tactical standpoint. Nobody else in the back line has his pace, composure or left-footed ball-playing ability.

Branthwaite adds balance, allowing Everton to push higher up the pitch and be more aggressive in their play. He brings comfort to those around him, sweeping up attacks down the left flank. Both left-back Vitalii Mykolenko and regular captain James Tarkowski appear to play better when he is on the pitch with them. There is no perfect solution with Branthwaite missing.

Michael Keane, who is trusted by Moyes and has improved this season, is the most likely direct replacement. At 33, he brings different elements to the table — including, ironically, a finishing ability similar to that of a striker — and already knew Tarkowski well from their time together at Burnley. But Moyes will now need to tighten up his defensive setup to guard against balls in behind and issues in transition.

A further injury to Keane or Tarkowski would almost certainly prompt a reshuffle, with Jake O’Brien shifting inside to his favoured role and a new right-back coming in. Were that to be recent England debutant and versatile midfielder James Garner, that would mean another change in the centre of the park. The lack of a permanent, favoured right-back, together with injuries, means Everton’s defensive resources are thinly spread.

In the long term, Everton must reduce their exposure to such injuries. They are likely to look to retain Keane, who is seen as a steadying presence by Moyes, beyond the end of the season, when his current contract expires. That deal includes a club option for a further year, should Everton wish to trigger it, instead of negotiating fresh terms.

A new right-back will also be targeted in the summer transfer window. That would allow Republic of Ireland international O’Brien to return full time to central defence, which is where he sees his future, and give Moyes a fourth option at that position.

Everton have invested heavily in Branthwaite, rejecting the overtures of Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, among others, in the past and signing him to a much-improved long-term contract last summer.

When The Friedkin Group completed its takeover in December 2024, the most likely scenario was that Branthwaite would be sold at the end of that season. But Moyes made the case that he wanted to build around Branthwaite, such is his talent. He is now one of Everton’s highest-paid players but has made just 10 Premier League appearances this season, seven of those starts.

Branthwaite struggled with thigh problems during previous manager Sean Dyche’s time in charge. But his recent issues have been hamstring-related and he has ended up locked in a cycle of injuries and setbacks. Everton tried to manage him carefully after his return to the squad in late January, keeping him out of certain games and training days, but that has not been enough.

In this new period, the focus will almost certainly be on getting to the bottom of what is going wrong and why. There are unlikely to be any easy answers.

Branthwaite’s tearful reaction at the weekend showed how heavily injuries can weigh on players — Premier League footballers are paid well but are still human. Being deprived of the ability to do what they love takes its toll.

He had returned to the side in fine form and was a standout performer in the derby before being forced off. Internally, there was a belief he was back to something approaching his best, making those dashed World Cup chances another bitter pill for him to swallow.

Branthwaite and Everton will now spend the next couple of months trying to find ways to end this cycle of misery.

text:
Unless there is a new rumor or move made, there is nothing new under the sun when it comes to the 2026 NFL draft. Until proven otherwise, despite a previous suggestion, many will assume that the Cleveland Browns are either drafting a wide receiver, an offensive tackle, and/or trading down in the first round of the draft.

We can mock draft in a million ways, including our more “win-now” version published on Wednesday morning, but the Browns will have to wait through a number of picks, with a shorter window between selections, to find out what GM Andrew Berry will do.

Given Berry’s NFL draft history, Cleveland fans are doubtful of this front office’s ability to make good decisions. In response to a big Myles Garrett trade package possibility, we saw this as the start of a response:

In no way do I trust the Browns in a draft.

That means, as this title indicates, fans are more likely to assume whoever Cleveland takes this year is the riskiest prospect to bust and whoever they pass over that they should have taken was the safest option. A look at the Top 25 prospects in the 2026 NFL draft, according to the Consensus Big Board, gives us this list:

QB Fernando Mendoza

LB Arvell Reese

Edge David Bailey

RB Jeremiyah Love

LB Sonny Styles

OT Francis Mauigoa

S Caleb Downs

WR Carnell Tate

Edge Rueben Bain

CB Mansoor Delane

OT Spencer Fano

WR Jordyn Tyson

WR Makai Lemon

OT Monroe Freeling

CB Jermod McCoy

iOL Olaivavega Ioane

TE Kenyon Sadiq

S Dillon Thieneman

OT Kadyn Proctor

Edge Keldric Faulk

Edge Akheem Mesidor

WR Omar Cooper Jr.

WR Kevin Concepcion

S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren

WR Denzel Boston

Trying to identify who is a risk and who is safe always starts with injuries. To some extent, those can’t be predicted, but there are indicators. Tyson, McCoy and Mauigoa have a history of concerns leading up to the NFL draft.

After injuries, where a player lands can often set them up for success or failure. Without any way to predict either injuries or landing spots, we are left with trying to just look at the prospects as they are.

Downs seems like the safest bet to be a very good player for a long time. After that, Love is the lone elite offensive prospect in this year’s group. On the risky side, Mendoza, as the first overall pick in a draft with no other top-level quarterbacks, could set him up for failure, while Reese’s tweener role at The Ohio State leaves room for the possibility of not reaching his potential in a specific role, and Bain’s short arms are historical outliers.

Proctor could be the biggest boom/bust prospect in the entire draft, with a chance to be a Top 5 left tackle or out of the league too soon (Alabama’s OLine history is very concerning).

For the Browns, the team needs talented players, but playing it safe could keep them from getting an elite prospect. There is never a right answer for a team that is trying to find its winning ways. If a safe pick is just good, not great, the upside is limited. If a risky pick busts, it is a waste of an opportunity.

title: My favorite Day 3 NFL Draft guys for the Bengals this year
description:
Fortunately for the Bengals, they have five Day 3 picks to use to bolster their offensive line depth.
Even after the Lawrence trade, the Bengals will use a lot of their early draft capital on defense.

text:
Ted Karras is one of the most optimistic people you’ll ever meet, and he’s as excited as anyone about the moves the Cincinnati Bengals have made this offseason.

“We’re a little bit light on O-Line numbers wise,” Karras said on Monday as he surveyed the Bengals’ roster after the Dexter Lawrence trade. “We’ll see if we have some nice additions and go get as good as we can this spring.”

Until Karras said it, I didn’t realize just how “light” the Bengals were.

The starting five is the best it has been in the Burrow era. Cody Ford and Jalen Rivers, who profile best as backup guards who can flex out to tackle in a true emergency situation, are the only other backups on the team with names that you’d recognize. We’ll see if Andrew Coker, Javon Foster and Jacob Bayer can turn any heads in training camp, but those aren’t guys who you go into camp with expecting to be on your roster.

Fortunately for the Bengals, they have five Day 3 picks to use to bolster their offensive line depth.

Even after the Lawrence trade, the Bengals will use a lot of their early draft capital on defense. One of the defining strategic questions of the draft for the Bengals will be how long they feel like they can wait for a swing tackle. That’s a glaring, red-flag need, and you don’t want to go in the season with a true backup guard (Ford/Rivers) being a snap away from playing tackle.

Offensive line could be the focus of the day on Day 3, and the Bengals need to come out of the draft with multiple offensive linemen (they also might need to sign an additional veteran). They could also look for a receiver to complement Mitchell Tinsley and develop in the background (in the Andrei Iosivas mold). The tight ends are interesting. And if there’s a defensive player who you like on Day 3, you’ll be able to find a role for him on a Bengals’ defense that still doesn’t have much depth at edge (Isaiah Foskey is DE5), linebacker (Shaka Hayward is LB4) or safety (PJ Jules is S4).

The Bengals don’t have a fifth-round pick but have two sixths and two sevenths.

Round 4 favorites

Miami OT Markell Bell. If you could guarantee now that Bell will be on the board in Round 4, that would probably give the Bengals a lot of reassurance. The best case scenario for this draft feels like defense in Rounds 2 and 3 and Bell in Round 4. He’s the classic big Bengals tackle, he didn’t allow a sack last year and he’s a winner.

Boston College OT Jude Bowry. A college captain who has the athleticism to be versatile and the size to set up shop at tackle. He has raw athletic tools to develop and size to play a role right away.

Oklahoma OL Febechi Nwaiwu. He has experience all across the line, Dane Brugler touted him as having some of the highest character in the draft and he’s a pass pro oriented player who can handle the power of the AFC North. He doesn’t cover a ton of ground, but he’s long and packs a punch. The Bengals reportedly showed plenty of interest during the pre-draft process.

Michigan OLB Jimmy Rolder. He’s a balanced athlete and a bit of a jack of all trades as a guy who can mix it up in the box or run around the field to chase a ball carrier. He has real athletic upside that he’s just tapping into, but he does need to clean up his tackling. He profiles as the combo linebacker/edge that they’re looking for, and he’d come at a bargain with the Bengals using a fourth-rounder there instead of a second-round pick.

Ohio State edge Caden Curry. While he was a very productive pass rusher in college, he projects in the NFL as a physical, tone setting defensive end who’s perfectly fine running full speed into tackles 50 times a game to seal off run lanes. The measurables aren’t great, but he’s physical. I also have a soft spot for defensive players who were used as fullbacks.

Oregon WR Malik Benson. My favorite Day 3 receiver. He runs downfield all day, tracks the ball incredibly well and was a big play machine. He might be more limited to just vertical routes, but he’s very good at them and would punish teams that leave him one-on-one against a No. 3 corner. Keep in mind as you’re scouting receivers that the Bengals hate guys who drop passes — Benson doesn’t. He also offers punt return value.

Florida corner Devin Moore. A sticky cover corner with the size, length and consistent tape that you’re looking for. He just has a very long injury history, missing half of the season in three of his four years of college.

Round 6 favorites

Florida LB George Gumbs. From walk-on wide receiver in the MAC to a five-sack defensive end in the SEC, Gumbs has one of the best stories in this class. Some view him as an undersized edge, but his background and his current physical frame suggest that Gumbs might be a better fit at linebacker. He looks like one, and the power, physicality, effort and ability to drop in coverage that he showed as a defensive end at Florida would all help him translate at linebacker. He can also help on special teams.

Arkansas guard Fernando Carmona. A versatile captain from the SEC with reps and experience who’s known for his anchor and ability in pass pro. Sounds like a Bengal.

Michigan State center/guard Matt Gulbin. He has a similar profile with the added ability to snap, which the Bengals need. In the transfer portal era, I’m really impressed with players who change schools and become a captain right away. His profile suggests that he’s a jack of all trades, master of none. He may be a long-term sixth man/backup on your line, but that’s a nice outcome for a sixth-round pick.

Wyoming guard Caden Barnett. He’s the best wrestler in this draft, which highlights some of his tools. He’ll have to make the small school jump, but his frame, aggressive style, ability to hold up against power and strength feels Cordell Volson-esque. That would be a successful outcome here.

Baylor WR Josh Cameron. A physical contested catch winner with traits worth betting on. He’s not a burner, but he can make the plays that Mitchell Tinsley did last year with his impressive strength, leap and terrific hands. He’s also a captain who returns punts.

Cincinnati WR Jeff Caldwell. The prototypical traits-based sixth-round receiver with elite height and speed combination.

Ole Miss TE Dae’Quan Wright. My favorite tight end in the draft. He generates splash plays, gets downfield for catches in the deep and intermediate passing game and was a focal point of his college offense. He’s a receiver-first tight end and would fit the Bengals in that way. He was versatile enough to line up in different spots, and he ranked second in the country in yards per catch. Dane Brugler also noted his improvements and toughness as a blocker.

USC edge Anthony Lucas. A five-star recruit who didn’t live up to expectations in college but is still relatively inexperienced as he got a late start to football. His traits, size, length and strength alone give him the ability to set the edge.

Round 7 favorites

Georgia guard Micah Morris. He was Dylan Fairchild’s backup and then took over that spot. He had to wait his turn on a stacked Georgia line, which cost him some reps and development. But he had the strength, power and potential to be in that mix in the first place.

Indiana center Pat Coogan. You’ve got to be smart to play center for the Bengals, and Coogan’s intangibles shined last year. Al Golden was with him for a few years at Notre Dame. He’s not the traitsiest, most nimble interior offensive lineman. But he’s tough, smart and has experience at guard. He has the raw size but is missing some length. Still, his track record said that he should have a chance to stick as a backup.

Nebraska safety/hybrid DB DeShon Singleton. His impressive combination of frame and athleticism instantly give him the look of an impact special teamer. As a team captain at Nebraska, he made a ton of plays in coverage on the ball, which is intriguing as well. Reports say that he also held his own in the slot, especially against tight ends. He feels like a guy who gives you depth in different spots and makes a career on special teams.

SMU tight end RJ Maryland. Remarkably fast. Son of former No. 1 overall pick Russell Maryland (a defensive tackle). Torn ACL in 2024 took away at his shot at a big breakout season in 2025, but his testing numbers showed a rare smooth athleticism for his position. Great down the seam, which would add something new to the Bengals. He also got plenty of snaps last year in the slot, which suggests an interesting potential to be a big, fast power slot who could make plays down the field and also make a big impact on special teams (like NFL veteran Ben Skowronek). Could provide a fun schematic wrinkle.

description:

text:
How the Cardinals judge their 2026 draft won't be known for a few years.

But their work ahead of the draft, at least in terms of shrouding it in mystery, has been impressive.

When the Cardinals are on the clock at No. 3 on Thursday night, the uncertainty – looking from the outside – is thick. Sure, a trade down is possible, but finding a partner was always going to be the issue. Cases can be made for either David Bailey or Arvell Reese as an edge rusher, or an offensive lineman like Francis Mauigoa, or even talented running back Jeremiyah Love.

Unlike 2024, when the Cardinals were choosing fourth and the selection of wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. seemed inevitable, this year's first round has a much different feel.

"The thing (coach) Mike (LaFleur) and I have talked about is we can never go wrong taking who we feel is the best player, who fits this team, (and) who is about what we're about," general manager Monti Ossenfort said. "When someone can check those boxes, we're going to be happy with that player, whatever position they're playing."

The key phrase there is "who fits this team." That addendum changes the equation.

Many analysts believe the best player in the draft is Love. The Cardinals signed Tyler Allgeier in free agency, they kept James Conner, they still have Trey Benson. And they have needs for a dynamic pass rusher and a right tackle.

When LaFleur was asked about taking a running back early – a Love question without a Love mention – the first-year head coach wasn't ruling anything out.

"I like what you're alluding to right there," LaFleur said. "I know I'm going to give you the political answer, but it's the truth. You just want to draft the best football player that's going to fit your team and what you're looking for, regardless of the position."

Love was asked by reporters in Pittsburgh on Wednesday about his potential future employer.

"I have no idea where I'm going, but there's a lot of talk of me going to the Titans, Cardinals, Giants," Love said. "Honestly, I'd be blessed to go anywhere."

Who the pick is at 3 is only one storyline the Cardinals are living in the moment. The trade, if someone wants to come up to 3 for an edge or Love, can't be ignored. What teams might be offering, however, will be the key in a draft that offers no real sexy reason (i.e. quarterback) to move up.

Then there is the Ty Simpson discussion. No one believes the Cardinals would take the Alabama quarterback at 3. But would he last until No. 34, the Cardinals' second-round choice, the second pick of the second round? Would the Cardinals trade back into the late second round to get him and take a chance at finding the quarterback of the future?

Even if the team stays at 3 and makes a choice by 5:30 p.m. Arizona time, the drama surrounding the team won't go away as the first round progresses.

The Cardinals have seven total picks. Regardless of when, getting an off-ball linebacker, an offensive lineman or two, a quarterback and another defensive lineman wouldn't be a surprise.

But the equation changes as names come off the board too, as does the lens through which the Cardinals see their needs.

"You can't just look at it like, 'Hey, how's this going to affect us tomorrow and the next day?'" Ossenfort said. "Every decision affects every decision moving forward. Our goal is to put as competitive of a team as we can to go into '26 and go 1-0 every week. That's what we're trying to do with the realization every decision we make affects subsequent years.

"I don't think those are two independent thoughts."

text:
PITTSBURGH -- NFL teams received a letter Wednesday about the progress of former Florida defensive tackle Caleb Banks as he recovers from a surgically repaired bone in his left foot.

The letter states that Banks underwent a CT scan Tuesday and is "on pace to be fully cleared for full football activities in early June," sources told ESPN.

The letter and timeline come after Dr. Norman Waldrop, a foot and ankle specialist with the Andrews Clinic, looked at Banks' scan. Banks had surgery March 9 on a fractured fourth metatarsal of his left foot.

Banks is among the top defensive tackles in this year's draft class, and a strong showing at the Senior Bowl in January bolstered his draft stock. But he suffered a broken bone in his foot at the NFL scouting combine in February, raising questions about his health after Banks played in just three games during the 2025 season at Florida because of an injury to the same foot.

Banks, who is 6-foot-6 and 327 pounds, is ranked among the top five defensive tackles in all of ESPN's draft analyst ratings. Both Jordan Reid and Field Yates rank him No. 3 at the position.

In 2024, Banks proved to be a dominant interior player in the SEC, finishing with seven tackles for loss, 4.5 sacks and two forced fumbles, and he entered the 2025 season as a second-team All-SEC preseason selection.

He played 12 games at Florida in both 2023 and 2024, logging 19 tackles and 1.5 tackles for loss in 2023.

title: 2026 NFL Draft red flags tracker: Prospects most likely to fall - CBS Sports
description:
Since no two prospects are the same, NFL Draft slides come in all shapes and sizes.
Here are the players in the greatest danger of sliding in the 2026 NFL Draft.
That could be a deterrent for NFL teams that need starting-level contributions right away.
Tyson held a personal workout for NFL teams on Friday, but was it enough to quell their concerns about his readiness for the pro level?

text:
Since no two prospects are the same, NFL Draft slides come in all shapes and sizes. For edge rushers, shorter arms often mean greater likelihood of slipping out of the first round. For quarterbacks, a lack of starting experience could be the difference between a Day 1 selection and a tumble into the middle rounds. The 2026 draft class could see both of those worries result in projected first-rounders falling out of the first 32 picks.

The 2025 draft provided one of the most infamous slides in recent memory as Shedeur Sanders, once viewed as a surefire first-round quarterback, waited all the way until Day 3 to hear his name called at No. 144 overall. It would be a true shock if any of this year's top prospects experienced that kind of disappointment, but then again, nobody expected it to happen to Sanders, either.

Just because a prospect missed an entire season due to injury or has character concerns does not mean teams will pass on him in the first round. These players are in the discussion to be among the first 32 players selected in the draft for a reason. All of them are potential stars. Teams have to weigh the risks with the possible stardom, though, and in some cases, it simply is not worth the investment.

The more red flags a player raises during the evaluation period, the more likely he is to plummet down the board. Reporting throughout the pre-draft process highlighted concerns for a bevy of potential first-rounders and we rounded them up into one list.

Here are the players in the greatest danger of sliding in the 2026 NFL Draft.

Rueben Bain Jr., EDGE, Miami

No edge rusher with an arm measurement of 30 7/8 inches or shorter has gone in the first round of any draft since at least 1999, per ESPN. While most expect Rueben Bain Jr. to snap that trend, the precedent exists for him to not only tumble out of the top 10 but to even wait until Day 2 to hear his name called.

Multiple defensive line coaches said to The Athletic that Bain's lack of arm length will force him to rely on his speed when he matches up against opposing tackles. Fortunately, he is well suited to do so. But it could make for a lengthy adjustment period, thus capping his rookie ceiling, and then what happens later in his career when he loses some of his athleticism?

Plus, while most teams consider the matter handled, Bain was cited in 2024 for careless driving in an incident that led to one passenger's eventual death. According to CBS Sports Lead NFL Insider Jonathan Jones, at least one team was not satisfied with Bain's explanation of the matter.

Cashius Howell, EDGE, Texas A&M

If Bain's arm length is an issue, then Cashius Howell is in an even more precarious position given that he measured out even shorter at 30 1/4 inches. He is more widely projected to be selected in the back end of the first round to begin with, so the risk of falling out of the top 32 is far greater than that of his Miami counterpart.

Howell developed into a standout after a year of development at both Bowling Green and Texas A&M, so while his measurables did not hold him back from elite production, he does have a history of needing time to get up to speed at various levels. That could be a deterrent for NFL teams that need starting-level contributions right away.

This week, Howell explained what he tells teams when they raise concerns about his size.

Francis Mauigoa, OT, Miami

An outstanding three-year Miami career, in which he earned Freshman All-American honors in 2023 and became a consensus All-American in 2025, suggests Francis Mauigoa has the upside to become the first offensive lineman selected.

At the same time, a back issue could scare teams away from making him a top-10 pick. Mauigoa was diagnosed with a herniated disc, per ESPN, and underwent a medical recheck two weeks ago.

While the injury is asymptomatic, it would require surgery if it gets worse. Plus, some teams think it is a matter of when, rather than if, he needs the procedure. These kinds of surgeries generally come with a three-month recovery timeline, so Mauigoa could have the procedure done this offseason and still be ready to go for Week 1. If he waits and the herniated disc worsens during the season, his rookie year could come off the rails.

Ty Simpson, QB, Alabama

This year's draft class lacks firepower at the quarterback position, which has left people searching for the next-best thing after Fernando Mendoza. While Ty Simpson has become the clear No. 2 passer behind the presumptive top overall pick, the gap between the two is arguably wide enough to keep him out of the first round. That would come as a surprise to some who think there are teams willing to trade up and grab him on Day 1.

Because the 2027 class projects as a loaded one at the signal-caller spot, teams have an incentive to wait another year before finding their franchise quarterback. That could spell a long wait for Simpson, Drew Allar, Garrett Nussmeier and the other quarterback prospects. Simpson having one year of starting experience at Alabama might be another deterrent, especially since he faded down the stretch of his 2025 campaign.

"I would not draft him in the first round, second round. I just don't know that he's going to be that good," one AFC executive said to NFL Media. "The longer you watch him, you feel a little man. What's he going to look like in our league? History's betting against us here. He gets thrown around. The kid's not very big, he's not very gifted. When he gets sacked, it looks like your dog swinging around their squeaky toy."

Renner's 2026 NFL Draft notebook: Red flags, sleepers and biggest questions in a wildly unpredictable class

Mike Renner

Jermod McCoy, CB, Tennessee

It doesn't take a whole lot of imagination to picture Jermod McCoy as an NFL standout, but it does take some. That's because he missed the entire college football season due to a torn ACL he sustained in January 2025.

What's more, NFL Media reports he could be headed toward another surgery. The ACL itself is reportedly in good shape, but a bone plug used to repair a cartilage defect in McCoy's knee may need to be replaced.

It has been well over a year since the Tennessee standout last played a snap, so even though he has participated in workouts and drills since then, there is no full guarantee that he is the same cornerback who flashed tons of potential in 2024.

McCoy was a terrific freshman at Oregon State and had a brilliant debut season in the SEC, and his tape screams "first-round pick." But now that he has an injury history and was limited to just two years of college ball, it would not be the biggest shock to see teams use their first-round capital elsewhere.

Jordyn Tyson, WR, Arizona State

Jordyn Tyson tore his ACL, MCL and PCL in 2022. He suffered a broken collarbone in 2024. A nagging hamstring injury limited him last season and caused him to sit out of the NFL combine and Arizona State's pro day. None of those injuries are directly related, but they paint a concerning picture that puts Tyson's durability in question.

Tyson held a personal workout for NFL teams on Friday, but was it enough to quell their concerns about his readiness for the pro level? The answer will come on Thursday when he either goes in the top half of the first round as expected or slips behind receivers with clearer outlooks.

ESPN reported Wednesday that the Cowboys like Tyson as a target with one of their two first-round picks, and longtime NFL team doctor David J. Chao explained why some teams are willing to overlook his string of injuries.

Kadyn Proctor, OT, Alabama

Only one prospect over the last 15 years weighed in at more than 350 pounds at the NFL combine and proceeded to go in the first round: Mekhi Becton in 2020. Kadyn Proctor projects to follow in his footsteps at 352 pounds.

This kind of size has its obvious benefits, and Proctor is immensely athletic for someone with his gigantic frame (he is also just under 6 feet, 7 inches). But it also has drawbacks, which were also apparent at Alabama -- where he was far from the most consistent blocker and saw his weight fluctuate -- and could lead to him moving inside to guard in the NFL.

That concern does not seem to faze front offices, as the draft week buzz suggests Proctor is in consideration to go in the top half of the first round. One AFC executive told ESPN that Proctor will go higher than people think.

Caleb Banks, DL, Florida

Recurring foot injuries are never ideal, but especially so for 327-pound linemen. Not only did Caleb Banks miss all but three games last season with a broken foot, but he also broke the fourth metatarsal in his left foot ahead of the NFL combine and underwent his second surgery in the span of six months.

According to ESPN, teams received a letter Wednesday concerning Banks' health. The defensive lineman underwent a CT scan on Tuesday, the letter states, which revealed enough healing to indicate he will be fully cleared for football activities in early June. While that is excellent news for his ability to play in 2026, it does not guarantee he will avoid further injuries.

Even with the foot issues, Banks commands hype as a first-round talent. He is a physical beast on the interior. The Florida product needs to stay on the field, though, because a lot of his allure revolves around his potential rather than what he put on the stat sheet in college. And there is plenty of room for teams to be concerned about his ability to do so.

title: Mel Kiper Says The Quiet Part Out Loud About Dante Moore's NFL Draft Decision
description:
Oregon Ducks quarterback Dante Moore shocked many with his decision to return to Eugene despite being projected as a top-five pick in the 2026 NFL Draft.
Mel Kiper Jr. On Dante Moore's NFL Draft Decision In many ways, Moore is the anti-cash out story.
That is exactly why Mel Kiper Jr. believes Moore's decision says something bigger about the new reality of college football.
Expect Moore's decision to continue to be discussed throughout the 2026 NFL Draft and the 2027 NFL Draft.
Dante Moore's Oregon Legacy Is Intensifying Moore's Oregon legacy isn't close to over.
text:
Oregon Ducks quarterback Dante Moore shocked many with his decision to return to Eugene despite being projected as a top-five pick in the 2026 NFL Draft.

There is no question NIL is changing draft decisions. The average age of prospects continues to rise as more players weigh another year of college football, another year of development and another year of NIL opportunities before entering the league.

However, Moore doesn't fit that bill. His decision was not driven by NIL. Moore potentially walked away from $40 to $50 million waiting for him in the league... because he believes another season at Oregon can make him a better quarterback and ultimately improve his long term future.

Mel Kiper Jr. On Dante Moore's NFL Draft Decision

In many ways, Moore is the anti-cash out story. Yes, the Ducks take care of him with a strong NIL package. But he had a big financial reason to leave and still chose to return to lead Oregon coach Dan Lanning's team.

That is exactly why Mel Kiper Jr. believes Moore's decision says something bigger about the new reality of college football.

“You’re getting paid to play college football. So why not stay and use that as kind of a minor league, a developmental league to make yourself a better player?” Kiper said.

It is the quiet part out loud... College football is a prep league for the NFL, and Lanning has also pointed that out in the past. This means, players are no longer forced to choose between getting paid and getting better. They can do both and Moore is the biggest example of that.

Moore staying at Oregon shows the Ducks are becoming college football’s ultimate quarterback launching pad. Between the elite facilities, coaching and national relevancy, Oregon gives Moore the environment to develop, win, and still protect his NFL future.

Instead of rushing out, more quarterbacks may start viewing one more season at the right school as the smarter move. This is evident in the 2026 NFL Draft, where Moore, LaNorris Sellers and Arch Manning all decided to return to school.

The other side of Kiper Jr.'s argument is the risk.

Every extra year in college gives a player more time to develop, but it also gives them one more season to suffer an injury that could hurt or even derail their NFL future. Of course, players can protect themselves with insurance policies designed to cover a career ending injury or a major drop in draft stock.

“And then, you’re always risking injury by playing another year. So that weighs on these kids’ minds. ‘Well, I had a good year. What if I got hurt?’ Again, there’s so many factors that go into it. That is not an easy decision to make," Kiper continued.

Expect Moore's decision to continue to be discussed throughout the 2026 NFL Draft and the 2027 NFL Draft. Moore's ceiling at Oregon is sky-high and Ducks fans can't wait to see him this fall.

Dante Moore's Oregon Legacy Is Intensifying

Moore's Oregon legacy isn't close to over. While the Detroit-native has flashed some incredible moments and exciting wins in 2025, there is more fun to be had on the horizon. It's clear that Moore is owning this season and taking the next step in his leadership for the Ducks, based on how his teammates speak about him.

Former Oregon tight end Kenyon Sadiq didn't hesitate when asked about Moore's decision to return to the Ducks football program. To Sadiq, it wasn't surprising, but it was revealing into just how unique the Ducks' starting quarterback is.

“I think it just speaks on the character he is as a person. Mentally, physically, all the things he took into consideration to make that decision to come back - I think it just more just speaks on who he is more than anything ... to see $40 million guaranteed and turn it down and come back to college for another year, I think takes a certain kind of person," Sadiq told Oregon Ducks on SI reporter Bri Amaranthus in an exclusive.

A now-healthy Oregon receiver Evan Stewart shared an emotional moment he shared with Moore when Stewart first learned of his season-ending injury.

"They told (Moore) the (injury) news and after I looked over and seen him crying, because basically he was kind of like kind of thinking it was his fault...But I was telling him like, what was going to happen was going to happen. It's not your fault. I a hundred percent want you to be my quarterback. Like the fact that you shed a tear, that really means a lot to me," Stewart said.

Stewart made it clear the tears weren’t weakness, they were proof of investment and how much Moore really cares about this team.

Moore looks to build off of a 2025 season that was one of the most efficient campaigns in the country. He ranked No. 3 nationally with a 72.9 completion percentage and No. 7 with a 166.73 passer rating.

Moore and the Ducks football team will again put on the pads for Oregon's spring game on April 25 in Autzen Stadium. The game will be broadcast live on the Big Ten Network, andadmission to the game is free.

It's the beginning of what could be a very special season with Moore at the helm.

title: How Long Victor Wembanyama Could Be Out With Concussion Based on NBA Protocol, Past Cases
description:
The Spurs lost Victor Wembanyama to a concussion on Tuesday night and then they lost Game 2 to the Trail Blazers.
Wembanyama, by rule, must sit out at least 48 hours after entering the concussion protocol.
He missed two days of practice but was back for the first game of the NBA Finals eight days later.
Justise Winslow suffered a concussion while with the Miami Heat and missed nine games over a three week stretch in 2019.
Nearly two weeks between games seems like the amount of time most football players take off after suffering a concussion.
text:
The Spurs lost Victor Wembanyama to a concussion on Tuesday night and then they lost Game 2 to the Trail Blazers. Now their concerns extend well past a series which is now tied 1-1 because they must weigh it against the longterm health of their star and the organization.

Wembanyama, by rule, must sit out at least 48 hours after entering the concussion protocol. With the series shifting to Portland on Friday there are three days between Game 2 and Game 3, which means he could play if he is cleared. But does San Antonio really want to put him on an airplane and rush him back even if he's feeling better in a couple days?

Letting him stay home while the team tries to win a game or two on the road seems like it would be the best decision for Wembanyama in both the short and long term and at the very least, the best interest of the franchise.

Here's how the rest of the series looks right now:

Spurs Remaining First Round Schedule

*if necessary

Past NBA Concussions

The most high-profile concussion in recent NBA history has to belong to Klay Thompson. During the 2015 playoffs he took a knee to the head from Trevor Ariza and had to leave Game 5 against the Rockets. Thompson was allowed to return to the game, but suffered symptoms, including dizziness and vomiting later that night. He missed two days of practice but was back for the first game of the NBA Finals eight days later.

Justise Winslow suffered a concussion while with the Miami Heat and missed nine games over a three week stretch in 2019. Donovan Mitchell missed more than two weeks when he suffered a concussion during the '22-'23 season. Jarrett Allen missed eight games with a concussion during the '21-'22 season.

Looking at how the Spurs handle concussions, both Jakob Poeltl and Jock Landale suffered concussions in the same game on Feb. 1 during the 2021-22 season. Landale returned to the court on Feb. 9 after missing two games. Poeltl, on the other hand, missed only one game before suiting up three days after suffering the concussion and played 32 minutes.

So when will Wemby return?

Every concussion is different, but there was no question Wemby suffered a head trauma in Game 2. He didn't try to shake it off and keep playing. Fans saw his chin bounce off the court and then he laid motionless for a moment before holding his head. He had trouble standing up at first and then ran straight to the locker room. Being cleared to return in as little time as possible would be unbelievable, but not in a good way.

The Spurs would be smart to be cautious, which should mean we won't see the Defensive Player of the Year for at least a couple games. In an ideal world the team could take care of the Blazers without Wembanyama and allow him to rest before a second round series against the Nuggets or Timberwolves, who seem destined to go seven games like they did in the 2024 playoffs.

Nearly two weeks between games seems like the amount of time most football players take off after suffering a concussion. It would seem like a lifetime for Wembanyama, but it might be the right thing to do.

text:
Predicting what GM Brad Holmes and the Detroit Lions do come draft time can be sort of a moot exercise. Each year, pundits take a look at the depth chart, attach the Lions to a prospect in that range based on the position he plays and file their mock draft without a second thought. And each year, Holmes and company reside in their office, chuckling over some of the names they’re linked to.

It’s a tale as old as time, and with the draft kicking off Thursday, expect more of the same.

Until then, here’s one final attempt at trying to predict where the Lions might go at No. 17.

Positions of need to monitor

The Lions, of course, don’t draft for need. But there is structure involved. They’ve drafted for need when it aligns with their board, which was the case in 2024. And you can often find them drafting for future needs, like they did a year ago when they selected Tyleik Williams to take over for DJ Reader in 2026.

With that in mind, it’s best to take a 50-foot view of this thing.

Offensive line: The Lions have two offensive line starters locked in for 2026 — center Cade Mays and right guard Tate Ratledge. The rest hasn’t been finalized. Is Penei Sewell making the switch to left tackle? The Lions signed Larry Borom in free agency, and Holmes is on record saying his best film is as at right tackle. A move like that could also open the door for the Lions to draft a young tackle in the first round. And while the Lions could let Christian Mahogany and Miles Frazier battle it out for the left guard spot and hope for development, what if a potential star is there?

Edge: The Lions have D.J. Wonnum slated to start at edge opposite Aidan Hutchinson, but it’s no secret they could use more. The front office has a type — players who can set a physical edge in the run game and win rushes consistently — but that could limit the number of true fits they’d select with Day 1 or 2 capital, as it has in past years.

Safety: If the Lions add a safety on Day 1 or 2 (or early Day 3), it could be viewed as a hedge on the health of Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (torn Achilles). In the event those two return to form, though, adding a starting-caliber safety with nickel flexibility could give the team an intriguing trio.

Linebacker: The Lions could use a linebacker now that Alex Anzalone is off to Tampa Bay, but what kind of linebacker? If they’re looking for a true one-for-one replacement in terms of skill set, they could be in the market for an athletic linebacker with the potential to develop into a strong coverage backer. There are a few on Day 2 and 3 who’d make sense.

Defensive tackle: The Lions lost Roy Lopez, and Reader isn’t expected back at this point. That’s a lot of muscle lost in the interior. And while Williams should take a step forward and Levi Onwuzurike will be returning from a torn ACL, could the Lions add another interior defensive lineman? Whether they go for a run-stuffing nose tackle, a pass-rushing three-tech or a combination, it would make sense to add another DT in either the draft or free agency.

Cornerback: Between Terrion Arnold’s name linked to an armed robbery/kidnapping case involving his friends, and D.J. Reed entering Year 2 of a three-year contract, could the Lions make it work with a first-round cornerback? Don’t be surprised.

Best first-round fits

Penn State G Vega Ioane: Arguably the best guard in the class, Ioane would give the Lions a Pro Bowl-caliber guard to slot in next to Sewell at left tackle (if he moves there). His film prep and no-nonsense demeanor would make him a strong culture fit. I was sold when I heard him at the combine. Poised, confident and in control.

Utah T/G Spencer Fano: Fano’s ability to offer quality play at either right tackle or left guard is incredibly enticing. While he projects as an NFL-ready right tackle, he could easily move to left guard for the 2026 season if the Lions believe Borom is one of their best five linemen. That positional flexibility could be the difference between him and another option. I wouldn’t be surprised if they go up to get him. One of my favorite prospects in the class, and a no-brainer if he’s there at 17.

Auburn edge Keldric Faulk: I’ve been on record for months now saying the Lions are going to have a hard time passing on Faulk if he’s available. He’s everything they’ve wanted in an edge rusher opposite Hutchinson. He’s long, powerful, versatile, mature, defends the run at a high level and has an excellent work ethic. He’s one of the younger prospects in the class and his upside is well worth the selection of a No. 17 pick.

Tennessee CB Jermod McCoy: Holmes wouldn’t draft a player coming off a torn ACL in the first round, would he? Surely that’s never happened before, right? One of the most gifted players in the class, McCoy should be on folks’ radar. The medicals will be key here, as it’s possible he slides like Will Johnson in 2025. But the talent is undeniable.

Georgia OT Monroe Freeling: A former five-star prospect, Freeling has tools for days and comes with the frame of a built-in-a-lab left tackle. One of the most athletic tackle prospects in relative athletic score history, Freeling will need time to develop, but his upside is immense. Starting to think he could be there at No. 17.

Clemson OT Blake Miller: In terms of pure culture fit, there might not be a better one than the Lions and Miller. When I heard the story about him delaying wrist surgery during spring practice to be available to his teammates, I knew he instantly checked that box. Then he tested and recorded an RAS of 9.90. Factor in his size, his 54 career starts and his character, you get a perfect fit.

Alabama G/T Kaydn Proctor: Proctor’s fit with the Lions is more of a stylistic one than anything. Players of his size aren’t supposed to move the way he does. Alabama lined him up at receiver on more than one occasion. He’s so young and still scratching the surface of what he could ultimately become, and projects as a mauling guard or a sturdy right tackle, if he keeps his weight in check and continues to develop. Will he ever get there? That’s a big if, but he could in the right situation.

Oregon S Dillon Thieneman: One of the cleanest evals in the draft, Thieneman is an elite athlete with a high IQ to boot. If he’s on the board at No. 17, he could check the BPA requirement as a do-it-all safety with positional versatility.

Toledo S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren: If the Lions are looking for a safety capable of creating game-changing plays, McNeil-Warren could be staring them down at 17. He’s mastered the art of the peanut punch and his versatility and physicality would be welcomed in this secondary.

Oregon TE Kenyon Sadiq: A tight end? In the first round? Again? The Lions, on a mission to add talent without locking themselves into specific positions, take the best player available. Sadiq could join forces with Sam LaPorta to create the most feared TE room in the NFL. Or he could replace him. LaPorta is entering the final year of his contract and watched his 2025 season end with back surgery. A move like this would be a fascinating wrinkle to that discussion.

My guys

Day 1: Ioane, Fano, Faulk, McNeil-Warren, Miami’s Ahkeem Mesidor, UCF’s Malachi Lawrence, Missouri’s Zion Young.

• I’m of the opinion that Lawrence sneaks into the first round. The more I’ve dug into his film, the more I question why he’s been mocked as a second-round pick. He’s got everything you want out of a first-round edge prospect. Size, arm length, speed, athleticism, a refined rush package and effort vs. the run.

• Meanwhile, Young’s violent nature should endear him to NFL teams, no matter where he lands.

• I just really love McNeil-Warren’s game. Think he’s going to help a defense immediately and his ability to get the ball on the ground is something that’s easier said than done. He does it. Consistently.

• I understand the concerns with Mesidor’s age, but it doesn’t bother me. He’s ready to go. I’m just not sure if the Lions will view him as a fit.

Day 2: Illinois edge Gabe Jacas, Pitt LB Kyle Louis, Texas Tech LB Jacob Rodriguez, Miami DB Keionte Scott, Arizona’s Treydan Stukes, Auburn edge Keyron Crawford, Georgia Tech G Keylan Rutledge, TCU S Bud Clark, Michigan edge Jaishawn Barham, Oklahoma’s Gracen Halton.

• If you’ve been following my draft coverage, you know that Louis is a favorite of mine. I really think his success will depend on where he goes, and it’ll take a smart defensive coordinator to find the right role for him, and the Lions have one in Kelvin Sheppard. He has the makings of a quality big nickel/weakside linebacker hybrid.

• Crawford simply hasn’t gotten enough love this cycle. Maybe it’s because he’s overshadowed by Faulk, but Crawford is a more refined pass rusher right now. He could be a steal for a team on Day 2.

• Barham would be a strong fit as a Sam linebacker in Detroit’s system — the hybrid linebacker/edge position. He could really grow into it over time. He intrigues me.

• If the Lions want to wait on a guard rather than taking Ioane, Rutledge could be their guy in the second. A true all-around guard with immediate starter written all over him.

• There are a ton of quality defensive backs there for the taking on Day 2, but my favorite is Scott. He reminds me so much of Devon Witherspoon — without the outside cornerback flexibility. He’s older at 25, but in the second round, that’s a player worth adding without hesitation.

Day 3: TCU LB Kaleb Elarms-Orr, Missouri DT Chris McClellan, Penn State RB Kaytron Allen, Utah TE Dallen Bentley, SF Austin CB Charles Demmings, Oregon LB Bryce Boettcher, Washington CB Ephesians Prysock, Iowa Edge Max Llewellyn, Kansas State DB VJ Payne.

• Day 3 is a good area to attack depth and add special teams contributors. Don’t sleep on the Lions adding a TE or a DB on this day. A ton of depth at those positions in this class.

title: The Jets did a lot of work on the 2026 NFL Draft QBs. Did they find one who fits?
description:
To recap: Between Geno and Geno, the Jets drafted five quarterbacks after the first round.
Still, the Jets have done work — a lot of work — on the rest of the top quarterbacks in this class in hopes of determining if any are worth drafting and developing.
The benefit of drafting a quarterback after Round 1 is that the Jets wouldn’t feel as obligated to play him as a rookie.
Reich is a former NFL quarterback who has been an offensive coordinator or head coach in the NFL since 2013, and he was a quarterbacks coach before that.
Any quarterback the Jets might look at after the first round is going to have flaws — some of them severe.
text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — If a quarterback drafted after the first round is a scratch-off lottery ticket, then the New York Jets have gone through a lot of losing tickets over the years.

They don’t have a rich history of drafting quarterbacks beyond Round 1 — though, they don’t have a rich history of drafting them in the first round either.

Thirteen years ago, the Jets drafted Geno Smith in the second round out of West Virginia. And now, 10 years after he departed at the end of a disappointing and tumultuous tenure, he’s back for another shot at leading the franchise.

Ten years ago, general manager Mike Maccagnan drafted Christian Hackenberg out of Penn State in the second round; he never played a snap for the Jets. Neither did Tajh Boyd, drafted in the sixth round in 2014 out of Clemson. Nor did James Morgan, a fourth-round pick out of Florida International in 2020. Jordan Travis was a sixth-round pick out of Florida State in 2024 — he retired in 2025 due to injuries, without ever even logging a practice in the NFL. Bryce Petty threw four touchdowns and 10 interceptions in 10 games after the Jets picked him as a fourth-rounder out of Baylor in 2015.

To recap: Between Geno and Geno, the Jets drafted five quarterbacks after the first round. They threw a combined 245 NFL passes, all by Petty.

That doesn’t offer much inspiration for a Jets franchise that appears to be on the brink of once again buying a scratch-off ticket and hoping for the best. Just because it hasn’t worked before doesn’t mean it isn’t worth trying again.

This is one of the stranger quarterback draft classes; the consensus is that only one QB has a first-round grade — and that quarterback (Fernando Mendoza) is already locked in as the No. 1 pick. Still, the Jets have done work — a lot of work — on the rest of the top quarterbacks in this class in hopes of determining if any are worth drafting and developing.

The benefit of drafting a quarterback after Round 1 is that the Jets wouldn’t feel as obligated to play him as a rookie. Many have tied the Jets to Alabama’s Ty Simpson — the consensus No. 2 quarterback in this class — simply because the Jets don’t currently have a long-term solution at the position and Simpson is viewed as a caliber of player who could become that solution one day.

Maybe the Jets believe that, though the knocks against Simpson (lack of size, inexperience, lack of arm strength) make it unlikely they’d use one of their current first-round selections (No. 2 and No. 16) on him. More likely, if he’s still there at No. 33 or 44, they’d consider him.

Whether they want him or not, the Jets have done extensive work on Simpson, just as they have on many other notable quarterbacks in this class. The Jets attended Simpson’s Pro Day at Alabama in March. Then a group of top Jets decision-makers — general manager Darren Mougey, head coach Aaron Glenn, offensive coordinator Frank Reich and quarterbacks coach Bill Musgrave — took him out to dinner and conducted a private workout the following morning.

At the NFL’s league meeting a few days later, Mougey said that “it was a good visit” with Simpson.

Over the course of the last few weeks, the Jets have also:

• Had dinner with Carson Beck in Miami prior to his Pro Day.

• Conducted a private workout with LSU’s Garrett Nussmeier.

• Hosted Penn State’s Drew Allar for a private workout.

• Met “extensively” with North Dakota State quarterback Cole Payton, according to a report, and hosted him on a top-30 visit.

• Spoke at length with Arkansas’ Taylen Green at the Senior Bowl and NFL Combine — and likely more since.

• Formally interviewed Behren Morton at Texas Tech’s Pro Day and hosted him for a top-30 visit.

And that’s just the information that has been unearthed.

For the quarterbacks who had private workouts with the Jets — most notably Simpson, Nussmeier and Allar — it is a true job interview. Mougey said the Jets will send the player a “kind of test” the night before and tell them to learn “all of this information,” the GM said.

The next morning, with Mougey, Glenn, Reich, Musgrave and the quarterback in a room, they quiz the player to see how much he retained from the night before.

The goal, said Mougey, “Let’s see how natural it is for you to talk football. Let’s see if we connect in the room personality-wise. And we’ll go through that meeting in the room, talking a lot of football, a little personal stuff, but a lot of their habits, just really getting a feel for their football mind, and then you go out into the field. Obviously, you see them physically, but at the same time, you’re kind of testing them mentally again.”

Glenn said at the owners’ meetings that he watches the quarterbacks during those workouts from the perspective of a defensive coach.

“If I’m a defensive player, how would I defend him? What are the issues we feel like he’ll have?” Glenn said. “Then we try to put him through drills. For example, we had one of our coaches, when one of our QBs drop back I want to attack him and see how he can maneuver in the pocket to get himself free to deliver the ball. Those are some things defensively I want to see.”

The flip side of that, Glenn said, is thinking from an offensive perspective — and evaluating the quarterbacks on the small details of things like how they handle dropbacks, three-step, five-step, under center, play-action and ball handling.

Glenn and Mougey are also leaning heavily on the expertise of Reich and Musgrave. Reich is a former NFL quarterback who has been an offensive coordinator or head coach in the NFL since 2013, and he was a quarterbacks coach before that. Musgrave has been a respected QB coach in the NFL across various franchises since 1997.

“It’s been great,” Mougey said. “Both Frank and Coach Musgrave were on the tour with us and got to go see some of these quarterbacks and it was awesome. Obviously, Frank and Billy have been around a long time, have evaluated a lot of quarterbacks, so there’s been a lot of good discussion.”

Glenn handed the keys to the offense to Reich when he hired him this offseason, allowing him to focus on calling plays on defense. So it would be fair to assume Mougey will be leaning on Reich for his opinions about this quarterback class and how they might fit into his offense.

Back in 2020, when he was coaching the Colts, Reich laid out five specific traits he looks for in quarterbacks, which is something to keep in mind when evaluating whom the Jets might pick this year at the position — if they pick anyone.

1. Toughness, mental and physical.

2. Accelerated vision. “That’s my wording for: How fast do you think on your feet?”

3. Accuracy: “You have to be really accurate in this league. The windows are small.”

4. Footwork: “You have to look for the feet. Most sports are played from the ground up. So as a quarterback, that’s really important, how you play with your feet.”

5. Intangibles: “The leadership. Are you a playmaker in big moments?”

So, considering those traits, which quarterbacks make the most sense for the Jets?

Simpson actually grades out well regarding those traits:

1. He played through injuries in 2025, though those injuries were a detriment to his performance.

2. In terms of “accelerated vision”, The Athletic’s Dane Brugler wrote that Simpson had a proclivity for holding onto the ball too long and second-guessing himself, often leading to sacks.

3. He only completed 64.5 percent of his passes in 2025, though his receivers did drop 25 passes, per Pro Football Focus.

4. NFL.com wrote that Simpson has “exceptional” footwork.

5. Simpson’s inexperience could work against him when it comes to intangibles — there’s not a big enough sample size to understand how he’ll handle himself when the games matter. And he struggled in the College Football Playoffs.

As for the others:

Garrett Nussmeier: He is lauded for his toughness and competitive edge, and Brugler wrote that he has “NFL-quality intangibles” as a leader. He completed 67.4 percent of his passes in 2025. He had the seventh-fastest average time to throw in 2025 (2.48 seconds, per PFF). Nussmeier does well under pressure and isn’t so much inaccurate as he is a gunslinger who is very willing to take risks. He has the zip to squeeze passes into tight windows, which sometimes leads to ill-advised throws while trying to make something happen.

Drew Allar: He has the size (6-foot-5, 228) that Reich typically prefers at quarterback, his arm strength is a plus and he’s well-respected by teammates, but he fell short in some of Reich’s other categories in college. Brugler wrote that Allar has “messy footwork,” “streaky ball placement,” “inconsistent rhythm,” and that he “sabotages himself with late decision-making.” He only completed 63.2 percent of his passes in four years.

Carson Beck: He also has the size (6-4, 233), significant experience (43 starts) and a history of being accurate (69.5 percent completions). Though he doesn’t have ideal arm strength, tends to struggle when his first read isn’t there, turns the ball over a lot (24 interceptions over the last two years), fumbles a lot (17 fumbles) and Brugler wrote that his “ball placement and decision-making plummet when eyes speed up and he gets flushed from original spot.”

Cole Payton: He is an inexperienced (13 starts) quarterback from an FCS school who has tantalizing athleticism (4.56 40, 40-inch vertical), a strong arm and is lauded for his toughness and leadership. Brugler also wrote that Payton has “inconsistent mechanics,” “gets frazzled under pressure” and has “underdeveloped pocket awareness.”

Taylen Green: He is another freak athlete — at 6-5 and 227 pounds, he ran a 4.36 40 and had a 43.5-inch vertical jump. He throws with legitimate arm strength and zip and was respected by teammates for his toughness and leadership. But he also has a funky delivery and inconsistent accuracy (60.1 percent completions, 35 interceptions in 53 games).

Any quarterback the Jets might look at after the first round is going to have flaws — some of them severe. They wouldn’t make it out of the first round if they were perfect.

The question is: Would the Jets put in all of that work into studying this quarterback class if they didn’t plan on drafting one?

title: 2026 NFL Draft: Why Carnell Tate 'No Doubt' Is the Best WR in the Class | FOX Sports
description:

text:
They tore the helmet off his head, but they couldn’t get the ball out of his hands. Two Wisconsin defenders could not stop Carnell Tate, who stood up and screamed in the end zone after catching a 33-yard touchdown pass to start Ohio State's 34-0 rout of the Badgers last October.

It was a touchdown that, technically, Tate shouldn’t have scored.

It should’ve been fellow OSU receiver Brandon Inniss’ TD. And yet when Inniss went down with an injury, then-Buckeyes offensive coordinator Brian Hartline did not hesitate to move Tate into the slot — just for one play — to make sure the execution was perfect. And that’s a testament to Tate, not just because the execution was perfect, but also because …

"He never practiced that play," Hartline, now the head coach at South Florida, told me earlier this month. "He may have seen it in practice, and he saw the other guys do it. But then you put him in the game and competitive excellence. The ball goes his way. He makes a huge play. So that's him as a player. He's always reliable to be put in the big spots."

Tate played in the slot during his freshman year in 2023, seizing an opportunity to get on the field after star receiver Emeka Egbuka suffered an injury. But since that point, Tate has been a perimeter receiver, which was why he hadn’t practiced that play prior to scoring the touchdown.

"Coach [Ryan] Day was like, ‘Hey, what do we do? Brandon's down. Where do you put who?’" Hartline recalled. "And I just said, ‘Listen, put Carnell in the slot. He'll know how to do it. He’ll do a great job on the route. We're good. Stay with the call.’ … We got a coverage that was good for us, and he went up and made a huge play over some defenders for a touchdown."

Tate is prepared for big spots — even when he shouldn’t be.

That’s one of many positive qualities the team that drafts the 6-foot-2, 192-pound receiver will get. But whichever team wants him the most, it'll surely have to be picking in one of the top 10 spots on Thursday night.

"I do it all," Tate told me in Portland at the Adidas "Pro Day" in March. "I run [routes], I block and I catch the ball. I run routes to get open at the highest level. I make contested catches, make good catches over the middle, and I go over top of people. Also, I add to the run game as well. I can impact the game with or without the ball."

Is he the best receiver in this year’s draft?

"Yessir. No doubt," Tate told me.

No hesitation whatsoever.

"I think it’s because of those things [I just mentioned] and also because of more of that," he added. "I feel like I'm the most intelligent receiver out there as well."

Though Arizona State's Jordyn Tyson is emerging as potentially the No. 1 receiver in this year’s class, it’s not all that controversial for Tate to stake his claim. And it's no surprise who Hartline is backing, calling Tate "by far the best receiver in this draft."

Ironically, Tate wasn't the WR1 at any point during his Buckeyes career. Ohio State bestowed that honor to Jeremiah Smith in 2025 and in 2024 and to Marvin Harrison Jr. in 2023. Egbuka was also firmly in the mix with more than 1,000 receiving yards in 2022 and 2024.

"[Tate] really wanted to be the guy. All the guys do," Hartline told me. "When you have a lot of guys in those rooms, sometimes it really makes you a better player when you understand the whole philosophy and where the ball goes. But I think he grew a ton as a person."

You can see the way Tate progressed simply by looking at the raw counting stats. He jumped from 18 catches, 264 yards and one touchdown in 2023 to 52 catches for 733 yards and four touchdowns in 2024. Then in 2025, he had 51 catches for 875 yards and nine touchdowns. It’s not staggering production. But his teammates never took him for granted.

"He’s a big-time receiver who’s gonna make a big play every day," Ohio State All-American edge Arvell Reese told me.

Tate’s draft prospects are a reminder of just how impressive he was in college — despite never being the top target. At Ohio State, that made for tough conversations when he battled to rise even into a WR3 spot in his sophomore year. Hartline and Tate spoke often about how to make it all work.

"I think that there's a lot of honesty. … I'm not gonna lie to the guys. And so if I tell you you're on track, and you just trust me on it, then that's the case," Hartline told me when asked how he managed Tate’s expectations. "I want everyone to have everything, because then there's no hard conversations. But ultimately, he was on pace. Keep trusting the process and the rest will take care of itself."

He added: "Happens all the time, right?"

Not to everyone.

It’s mostly true for the Ohio State locker room, which is a big reason why Hartline is set to start his first season as the head coach for USF. Before Smith, Tate, Egbuka and Harrison Jr., there was Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Garrett Wilson and Chris Olave. Hartline has continued to produce elite pass-catchers, with Tate appearing to be next in line.

This OSU assembly line has created a pro-ready mentality. Not only will these players sharpen each other’s skills off the field, but they’ll have the self-assurance and self-discipline to fight their way to the top of a pro-caliber depth chart.

"They're surrounding themselves with great players, and although frustrating, it's going to be frustrating in the league too. Better get ready for it," Hartline said. "So understanding that, we always want more [production], but that's not how this works. They do a really good job at our job description on each individual play."

Whether Tate lands in Cleveland, Kansas City or any of the other top-10 slots, he'll have to beat out tough competition for a top starting spot. But there's little doubt he'll do just that. He'll do what it takes to make an impact, even if that means jumping into a position he's never practiced — and on the play that matters most.

text:
Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite is unlikely to play again this season after sustaining a hamstring injury in Sunday's Merseyside derby defeat.

The centre-half was in tears as he left the pitch on a stretcher in the 87th minute of Everton's 2-1 loss to Liverpool at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

After the match, the 23-year-old was seen leaving on crutches and Everton boss David Moyes said he was concerned the injury "could be serious".

Branthwaite missed the first five months of the season - having hamstring surgery in October - and returned to the side in January.

However, his latest injury is unrelated and a scan shows he does not require an operation, Everton said.

He will now start his rehabilitation at the Toffees' Finch Farm training ground, the club added, external.

The injury is a blow to Branthwaite's World Cup hopes, as England's tournament starts on 17 June against Croatia in the United States.

He made his senior debut in a friendly against Bosnia-Herzegovina two years ago but missed out on the Three Lions' 26-man squad for Euro 2024.

text:
Yes, he is raw. Yes, he will have growing pains. But the most exciting thing about Iheanachor as a prospect is that you can easily see how he has progressed in his few short years of playing football, and there is no reason to think that progression will stop. I think Iheanachor has the highest ceiling of any offensive tackle in the class, and if he hit's that ceiling, the Browns will be set for a decade or more.

Round 2 – Pick 39: D'Angelo Ponds, CB Indiana

This is my draft crush. This is my Draft Day, "D'Angelo Ponds no matter what." This kid is an absolute star. Yes, let's get it out of the way, he's 5'9 if he's wearing tall cleats and only 180 pounds. Does that give me pause here? Not even for one second. Go watch the hell he put Jeremiah Smith through. Go watch what he did to Denzel Boston. Look at what he has done to the cream of the crop receivers he has lined up across from all season long. There's no way this kid's size will impair his abilities because his abilities are flat out elite. His cover skills are elite. His ball skills are even better. And then you throw in his return abilities, and D'angelo Ponds instantly makes the Browns a better team.

Round 3 – Pick 70: Germie Bernard, WR Alabama

Since the beginning of the draft season, I have said that I want the Browns to wind up with 2 receivers after their first 4 picks, and Bernard would be a really

solid grab here in the third round.

Bernard brings much of what I love about Carnell Tate to the table. He's a crisp, savvy route runner, he's a smart player in reading a defense and always being where he needs to be, and he's about as sure-handed as it gets, dropping only 4 balls on 232 career targets. He does lack the physicality and strength of Tate, which is why he's available at this point, but while Tate is going damage on the boundaries, Bernard gives you a reliable threat who thrives over the middle of the field.

Put Tate on the outside and interchange Jeudy and Bernard on the other side and in the slot and you have dramatically improved your wide receiver room heading into next season.

Round 4 – Pick 107: Jalon Kilgore, S South Carolina

No, this isn't the true centerfielder type safety prospect the Browns have long searched for, but Jalon Kilgore gives the Browns something else they covet dearly – he is one of the most versatile defensive backs in this class. Kilgore has been a standout player for a couple years now in the SEC as a player that South Carolina basically just designed a position for.

He spent some time as a free-ranging safety in certain situations, and his ability to read a quarterback really stood out. In other situations, he was asked to be abox safety, and his physicality and brutal playing style stood out. And in other situations he was asked to slide to nickel, and his coverage skills and ability to win at the point of attack stood out.

The point is, no matter where Jalon Kilgore was playing, he stood out. That's the kind of player I want rounding out the Browns secondary.

Round 5 – Pick 146: Eli Raridon, TE Notre Dame

As the Browns continue to revamp their tight end room, they find a player built in the mold of what they're searching for in Raridon out of Notre Dame. The 6'6" 250 pounder once again adds that versatility we often see Andrew Berry attracted to. Raridon can line up as the in-line tight end, but he has incredible athleticism,

speed, and explosiveness to get off the line and make big plays in the receiving game. While his skinny-ish frame may scare some people in the run-blocking area, he's been a very good run blocker throughout his career.

Really, the biggest concern about Raridon may be the fact that he tore his ACL his senior year in high school, and then he re-tore it at Notre Dame. Two catastrophic

knee injuries to the same knee is certainly reason for pause. But Raridon has now bounced back and played two consecutive full seasons, showing that he is absolutely an NFL caliber tight end.

Round 5 – Pick 149: Red Murdock, LB Buffalo

Welcome to the late-round players I absolutely adore portion of this mock, and it starts with potentially the most violent player in this draft class, Red Murdock. Murdock is a tackling machine, finishing each of the last two seasons in the top two of all linebackers in the nation in tackles. But it's not the tackles that tell the story for Murdock. It's the 30-plus tackles for a loss over the last two years.

It's the game breaking interceptions. And it's his signature stat – fifteen forced fumbles over the last 2 years, which were the most in the nation. Murdock is not the perfect player. He struggles in pass coverage, sometimes badly, and he's not the sideline-to-sideline speed type of linebacker we've fallen in love with here in Cleveland recently. But his knack to make big plays in the backfield and his bone-crushing hits that so frequently pop the ball loose are traits worth taking a chance on here in the 5th round.

Round 6 – Pick 206: Landon Robinson, DT Navy

And we will conclude the late-round players I absolutely adore portion of this mock here with Landon Robinson out of Navy. Robinson will fall this far, and perhaps farther, because of his measurables. He's 5'11 and 293 pounds with 31 inch arms. Robinson is this year's Adin Huntington, for me. If you're going to look at the measurables and determine that he won't be good based on those, then you're going to miss out on a really solid prospect who just might make you look like a brilliant GM if you take him.

Robinson is an explosive interior defensive lineman who, by then end of his time at Navy, made a living in the backfield racking up tfls and sacks. He is much stronger than his frame suggests, and would be yet another problem for Browns opponents to have to deal with, especially in obvious passing situations.

Round 7 – Pick 248: Micah Morris, OL Georgia

Let's start with this – I don't believe for one second that Andrew Berry will make this pick. I think we will see one of the patented 7th rounder for a 6th rounder next year pick swaps that we've seen many times before. Having said that, I went ahead and brought in a player with this pick, and I went with Micah Morris, the 6'5 334 pound monster out of Georgia. The gameplan for Morris is simple. He needs coaching. Many of his flaws are mental, where he just doesn't make the right read, or recognize how the defense is lining up, and then he's late to react.

At the same time, he's got that mauler mentality, especially when run blocking, that you want out of a guard along the line. His athletic profile is shockingly good for a player of his size, and there is plenty of film that shows him looking dominant at times against SEC opponents. With some short-term solutions the Browns currently have on the interior line, Morris would be a worthwhile swing on a long-term solution if developed properly.
